questions.stem: Which sequence correctly shows a stimulus-response model?
options: Stimulus, effector, control centre, receptor, response
Receptor, stimulus, effector, control centre, response
Stimulus, control centre, receptor, response, effector
Stimulus, receptor, control centre, effector, response
questions.explanation: A receptor detects the stimulus and sends a message to a control centre, which signals an effector such as a muscle or gland to produce a response. The effector acts after, not before, the control centre.

questions.stem: In a homeostatic control system, what makes a response an example of negative feedback?
options: The response counteracts the change that triggered it
The response increases the change that triggered it
The response continues even after conditions return to normal
The response happens only when the stimulus is harmful
questions.explanation: In negative feedback the response reverses the original change, returning the variable towards its set point. A response that amplifies the change is positive feedback.

questions.stem: In vertebrates, how do the nervous and hormonal pathways that link receptors to effectors usually differ?
options: Nervous responses travel in the blood to all cells
Hormonal responses use electrical impulses in axons
Nervous responses are faster and shorter-lasting
Hormonal responses are faster and more localised
questions.explanation: Nerve impulses travel quickly along neurons to specific effectors, giving rapid, brief responses. Hormones travel in the blood, so their effects are slower to start but last longer and can affect many tissues.

questions.stem: In the control of body temperature, which structure acts as the control centre?
options: The skeletal muscles
The hypothalamus
The sweat glands
The skin thermoreceptors
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus compares information from thermoreceptors with the set point and sends messages to effectors. Sweat glands and muscles are effectors, and thermoreceptors are receptors.

questions.stem: What carries a nerve impulse along an axon?
options: A hormone carried in the blood beside the axon
A flow of electrons along the outside of the axon
An action potential, a moving change in membrane charge
A neurotransmitter that diffuses down the inside of the axon
questions.explanation: A nerve impulse is an action potential: a brief reversal of the charge across the axon membrane that travels along it. Neurotransmitters act only at synapses, between neurons.

questions.stem: What causes the inside of an axon to become positive during an action potential?
options: Neurotransmitter molecules enter the axon from the synapse
Sodium ions rush into the axon through opened channels
Potassium ions rush into the axon through opened channels
Chloride ions leave the axon through opened channels
questions.explanation: When the membrane is stimulated, sodium channels open and positive sodium ions flood in, depolarising the axon. Potassium ions then move out, restoring the negative resting charge.

questions.stem: Which event occurs when an action potential reaches the end of a presynaptic neuron?
options: Sodium ions diffuse across to the next neuron
Hormones are released from the axon into the bloodstream
Neurotransmitter is released into the synaptic cleft
The impulse jumps electrically across the cleft
questions.explanation: The arriving impulse causes vesicles to release neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft. It diffuses across and binds to receptors on the next cell, which may start a new impulse there.

questions.stem: Why can a nerve impulse pass across a synapse in only one direction?
options: The synaptic cleft is too narrow for impulses to pass back the other way
Neurotransmitters are broken down as soon as they leave the presynaptic neuron's terminal
The axon membrane of the presynaptic neuron cannot be depolarised a second time
Only the first cell releases neurotransmitter, and only the next cell has receptors
questions.explanation: Vesicles of neurotransmitter are found only in the presynaptic terminal, and the receptors only on the postsynaptic membrane. The signal can therefore only cross from the first cell to the next.

questions.stem: In signal transduction, what happens after a signalling molecule such as a hormone binds to a receptor on a target cell?
options: The receptor breaks down and the cell stops responding
The hormone is converted into a new nerve impulse
The cell releases the hormone back into the blood unchanged
A series of changes inside the cell leads to a response
questions.explanation: Binding to the receptor starts a chain of events inside the cell, such as activating enzymes, which ends in a response. The signal is transferred into the cell rather than the hormone being turned into an impulse.

questions.stem: A drug blocks the receptors for a neurotransmitter on a muscle cell. What is the most likely effect when the motor neuron fires?
options: The muscle contracts more strongly, because more transmitter is released
The muscle responds normally, because the impulse jumps the cleft
The neuron stops producing action potentials along its whole axon
The muscle does not respond, because the signal cannot cross to it
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitter must bind to receptors on the postsynaptic cell to pass the signal on. With the receptors blocked, the impulse in the neuron cannot trigger a response in the muscle, even though the neuron still fires.

questions.stem: How do most animal hormones reach their target cells?
options: They are secreted by endocrine glands into the blood or lymph
They are carried along axons from the brain to each target cell
They are released through ducts directly onto the target
They diffuse from cell to cell through the body tissues
questions.explanation: Endocrine glands are ductless; they release hormones into the circulatory or lymph system, which carries them throughout the body. Glands with ducts, such as sweat glands, are exocrine glands.

questions.stem: A hormone circulates to every part of the body, yet only affects certain cells. Why?
options: Only target cells are linked directly to the gland by neurons
Only target cells have receptors specific to that hormone
Only target cells are close to the gland that makes it
The hormone is broken down before reaching most cells
questions.explanation: A hormone acts only on cells with receptors whose shape matches it. Other cells are exposed to the hormone but cannot respond, because they lack those receptors.

questions.stem: How do hormones bring about their effects on target cells?
options: They supply the energy the cells need to function
They replace the DNA of the target cells
They carry nerve impulses directly into the cells
They increase or decrease the activity of the cells
questions.explanation: Hormones alter the metabolism of target cells, tissues or organs by speeding up or slowing down particular processes. They are signals, not an energy source or genetic material.

questions.stem: On a hot day a cyclist's skin turns red and she sweats. How do these responses lower body temperature?
options: Vasoconstriction lowers the heart rate and sweat insulates the skin
Vasodilation brings blood to the skin and sweat removes heat as it evaporates
Vasoconstriction keeps blood near the skin and sweat adds an insulating cooling layer
Vasodilation moves blood to the core and sweat blocks heat from entering
questions.explanation: Arterioles supplying the skin dilate, so more blood flows near the surface and loses heat. Evaporating sweat absorbs heat from the skin. Vasoconstriction is the response to cold.

questions.stem: Which set of responses helps raise body temperature in a cold environment?
options: Shivering, vasodilation in the skin and more sweating
Panting, vasoconstriction in the skin and lowered metabolic rate
Shivering, vasoconstriction in the skin and raised metabolic rate
Sweating, vasodilation in the skin and lowered metabolic rate
questions.explanation: Shivering and a higher metabolic rate generate heat, while vasoconstriction reduces blood flow to the skin so less heat is lost. Sweating and vasodilation would increase heat loss.

questions.stem: A person's core temperature rises after exercise, and the response returns it to normal. Which statement correctly describes the feedback loop?
options: Thermoreceptors detect the rise, the hypothalamus signals sweat glands, and sweating stops once temperature falls
Sweat glands detect the rise, the hypothalamus releases sweat, and sweating continues until it is cold
The hypothalamus detects the rise, the skin signals the brain, and blood vessels in the skin constrict to lose the heat
Thermoreceptors detect the rise, the pancreas signals the skin, and shivering removes the extra heat
questions.explanation: Receptors detect the change, the hypothalamus acts as control centre and signals effectors such as sweat glands, and once temperature falls back to normal the stimulus is removed and the response stops. That switching off is what makes it negative feedback.

questions.stem: Which hormone is released when blood glucose concentration rises after a meal?
options: Glucagon
Antidiuretic hormone
Adrenaline
Insulin
questions.explanation: Beta cells in the pancreas detect high blood glucose and release insulin. Glucagon is released when blood glucose falls, and ADH controls water reabsorption.

questions.stem: How does insulin lower blood glucose concentration?
options: It increases glucose uptake by cells and conversion to glycogen
It increases the breakdown of glycogen in the liver to glucose
It causes the kidneys to excrete all the glucose in the blood
It stops the small intestine from digesting any carbohydrate
questions.explanation: Insulin makes body cells take up more glucose and stimulates the liver and muscles to store it as glycogen. Breaking glycogen down to glucose is the effect of glucagon, which raises blood glucose.

questions.stem: Several hours after eating, a student's blood glucose falls below normal. Which response restores it?
options: The pancreas releases glucagon, and the liver converts glucose into glycogen
The liver releases insulin, and muscles convert glycogen into glucose
The pancreas releases glucagon, and the liver breaks glycogen into glucose
The pancreas releases insulin, and the liver breaks glycogen into glucose
questions.explanation: Alpha cells in the pancreas release glucagon when blood glucose is low. Glucagon causes the liver to break down stored glycogen and release glucose into the blood.

questions.stem: A person's pancreas cannot produce insulin. Which outcome is most likely after a carbohydrate-rich meal?
options: Blood glucose stays high because cells take up little glucose
Blood glucose falls quickly because glucagon is not released
Blood glucose stays normal because glucagon lowers it instead
Blood glucose falls because the liver stores the extra glucose
questions.explanation: Without insulin, cells take up little glucose and the liver stores little as glycogen, so blood glucose remains high. This is what happens in type 1 diabetes. Glucagon raises blood glucose; it cannot lower it.

questions.stem: Which hormone controls the amount of water reabsorbed by the kidneys?
options: Glucagon
Thyroxine
Antidiuretic hormone (ADH)
Insulin
questions.explanation: ADH, released from the pituitary gland, increases water reabsorption in the nephron. Insulin and glucagon regulate blood glucose, and thyroxine affects metabolic rate.

questions.stem: After a long run without drinking, a runner's blood becomes more concentrated. Which response follows?
options: Less ADH is released, so less water is reabsorbed and urine is concentrated
More ADH is released, so more water is reabsorbed and urine is concentrated
Less ADH is released, so more water is reabsorbed and urine is dilute
More ADH is released, so less water is reabsorbed and urine is dilute
questions.explanation: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the concentrated blood, and more ADH is released. ADH makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water, so more is reabsorbed and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced.

questions.stem: Where in the nephron does ADH act?
options: The renal artery leading to the glomerulus
The distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct
The glomerulus and Bowman's capsule
The proximal convoluted tubule only
questions.explanation: ADH increases the permeability of the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct to water. Filtration happens at the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule, and most bulk reabsorption in the proximal tubule is not controlled by ADH.

questions.stem: What happens at the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule of a nephron?
options: Glucose is actively added to the urine
Urine is stored before it leaves the body
Blood is filtered under pressure, forming filtrate
Water is reabsorbed under the control of ADH
questions.explanation: High blood pressure in the glomerulus forces water and small solutes into Bowman's capsule, forming filtrate. Blood cells and large proteins stay in the blood.

questions.stem: In a healthy person, glucose is present in the filtrate in Bowman's capsule but not in the urine. Why?
options: It is converted to glycogen in the collecting duct
It is reabsorbed into the blood in the proximal convoluted tubule
It is too large to pass from the glomerulus into the capsule
It is broken down by digestive enzymes as it passes along the loop of Henle
questions.explanation: Glucose is small enough to be filtered, but it is all reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule. Glucose appears in urine only when blood levels are so high that reabsorption cannot keep up.

questions.stem: The kidneys filter about 180 L of fluid from the blood each day, and about 1.8 L of urine is produced. What percentage of the filtrate is reabsorbed?
questions.explanation: The fraction lost as urine is 1.8 ÷ 180 = 0.01, or 1%, so 100% − 1% = 99% is reabsorbed. Subtracting 1.8 from 100 treats litres as if they were percentages.

questions.stem: Drinking alcohol reduces ADH release. What effect does this have on urine and blood?
options: Small volumes of concentrated urine and a risk of overhydration
Large volumes of concentrated urine and more water in the blood
Small volumes of dilute urine and no change in water balance
Large volumes of dilute urine and a risk of dehydration
questions.explanation: With less ADH, the collecting ducts are less permeable to water, so less is reabsorbed and a large volume of dilute urine is produced. The body loses water, which can lead to dehydration.

questions.stem: Which tissue carries water from the roots to the leaves of a plant?
options: Phloem
Epidermis
Mesophyll
Xylem
questions.explanation: Water and dissolved minerals move up the plant in xylem vessels. Phloem carries sugars, and the epidermis and mesophyll are leaf tissues.

questions.stem: What is the main force pulling water up the xylem of a tall tree?
options: Transpiration from the leaves creating tension in the water column
Root pressure pushing water all the way up to the top of the tallest tree
Active pumping of water by living xylem cells along the stem
Gravity drawing water upwards from the soil into the leaves
questions.explanation: Evaporation of water from the leaves pulls on the column of water in the xylem, and cohesion transmits the pull down to the roots. Root pressure contributes only a small push, not enough for tall trees, and mature xylem cells are dead.

questions.stem: Why does the column of water in the xylem not break as it is pulled upwards?
options: Water molecules are attracted to each other by cohesion
Water molecules are actively pumped by xylem walls
Root pressure fills any gap that forms in the column
Sugars in the xylem hold the water molecules together
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonds attract water molecules to each other (cohesion), so the column holds together as a continuous thread under tension. Adhesion to the xylem walls also helps.

questions.stem: What is root pressure?
options: A push from soil water forced into roots by the weight of the soil
A pull from phloem, as sugar movement drags water down to the roots
A push from roots, as ions pumped into the xylem draw water in by osmosis
A pull from the leaves, as evaporation through open stomata draws water upwards
questions.explanation: Root cells actively move mineral ions into the xylem, lowering its water potential, so water enters by osmosis and builds up pressure. It is a push from below, unlike the transpiration pull from the leaves.

questions.stem: A potometer shows a plant's rate of water uptake. Which change would most likely decrease the rate?
options: Raising the humidity of the air around the leaves
Turning a fan on to blow air across the leaves
Increasing the light intensity on the leaves
Raising the air temperature from 15 °C to 25 °C
questions.explanation: High humidity reduces the gradient between the moist air spaces in the leaf and the outside air, so less water evaporates. Wind, brighter light (which opens stomata) and warmer air all increase transpiration.

questions.stem: In a potometer, an air bubble moves 30 mm in 10 minutes along a capillary tube with a cross-sectional area of 0.5 mm². What is the rate of water uptake?
options: 3 mm³ per minute
15 mm³ per minute
6 mm³ per minute
1.5 mm³ per minute
questions.explanation: The volume taken up is 30 mm × 0.5 mm² = 15 mm³, and 15 mm³ ÷ 10 min = 1.5 mm³ per minute. Forgetting to divide by time gives 15, and forgetting the area gives 3.

questions.stem: Which feature of a xerophyte reduces water loss from its leaves?
options: Stomata sunken in pits and surrounded by hairs
Large, thin leaves with many exposed stomata
A thin cuticle that lets light reach the cells
Stomata that stay open throughout the hot day
questions.explanation: Sunken stomata and hairs trap a layer of humid air, reducing the gradient for evaporation. Large thin leaves, a thin cuticle and open stomata in heat would all increase water loss.

questions.stem: Some desert plants open their stomata only at night and store carbon dioxide for use during the day. What type of adaptation is this, and how does it save water?
options: Behavioural: the plant moves its leaves into shade to stop evaporation
Physiological: the plant takes in water through its stomata at night
Physiological: gas exchange happens when it is cooler and less water evaporates
Structural: the stomata are much smaller at night, so less water vapour can escape
questions.explanation: Changing when stomata open is a physiological adaptation. At night the air is cooler and more humid, so far less water is lost while carbon dioxide enters. Stomata release water vapour; they do not absorb liquid water.

questions.stem: A desert hopping mouse stays in a burrow during the day and feeds at night. What type of adaptation is this?
options: Structural
Physiological
Hormonal
Behavioural
questions.explanation: Staying underground by day and being active at night is behaviour that avoids heat and reduces water loss. Producing very concentrated urine would be a physiological adaptation, and long loops of Henle are structural.

questions.stem: Desert mammals often have nephrons with very long loops of Henle. How does this help them conserve water?
options: It stops ADH from acting, so less water enters the urine
It adds more salt to the urine, so the urine becomes more dilute than blood
It builds a steeper salt gradient, so more water is reabsorbed
It filters more blood, so more water stays in the body
questions.explanation: Long loops of Henle build a high salt concentration in the kidney medulla. Water then leaves the collecting ducts by osmosis, giving very concentrated urine and little water loss.
